client: I've been having a really hard time since my grandmother passed away last year. Every time there's a family get-together, I just... find reasons not to go, because being there without her feels unbearable. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: It takes real courage to show up here, even when part of you isn't sure it will help — and I want you to know that ambivalence is completely okay. The pain of losing your grandmother and then facing those family gatherings without her sounds genuinely heartbreaking, like her absence becomes most visible in the very places she used to be most present. I'm curious — when you imagine walking into one of those get-togethers, what's the thought that feels the loudest or most difficult to sit with?

client: I think the loudest thought is something like... "everyone else has moved on, and I'm the only one still falling apart." Like I'll walk in and people will be laughing and talking normally, and I'll just be standing there feeling her absence like this huge weight that no one else seems to notice. It makes me feel really alone, even surrounded by my own family.
therapist: That thought — "everyone else has moved on and I'm the only one still falling apart" — sounds like it carries a lot of quiet pain, almost like grief is isolating you even in a room full of people who loved her too. It's worth gently asking: is there any evidence that others in your family *aren't* still carrying their own weight of missing her, even if they're not showing it the same way you are? I wonder, has there been any moment — even a small one — where someone else let their grief show?

client: Actually... yeah, I remember my aunt tearing up when someone mentioned my grandmother's famous apple cake at Thanksgiving. She tried to cover it up pretty quickly, but it was there. I guess I noticed it but then kind of dismissed it, like I told myself she was fine and I was the one making it into a bigger deal than it needed to be.
therapist: That moment with your aunt is really significant — she felt it too, and your instinct *did* notice it, even if another part of you quickly talked you out of trusting what you saw. It's interesting how the same mind that caught her grief then turned around and used it as evidence that *you* were the problem, rather than that you were both just two people missing the same woman. What do you think it would mean for you if the people at those gatherings were actually more like you than you've been allowing yourself to believe?

client: I think it would mean I don't have to keep carrying this alone, which honestly sounds like a relief but also kind of terrifies me. Like if I let myself believe that, then I'd have less reason to keep avoiding the gatherings, and actually showing up feels really scary. I'm not sure I'm ready to stop protecting myself that way, even if the protection is also what's keeping me isolated.
therapist: What you just said shows a lot of self-awareness — you can see both sides of this so clearly, that the avoidance is both protecting you *and* costing you something real, and that's not a small thing to recognize. It makes complete sense that letting go of a coping strategy, even one that's keeping you stuck, would feel frightening rather than just relieving. I'm wondering — when you imagine "showing up" to a gathering, is it more scary to be seen in your grief by others, or to allow yourself to feel the full weight of her absence in that space?

client: Honestly, I think it's more scary to feel the full weight of her absence in that space, because at least if someone sees me upset, I can kind of brush it off or excuse myself. But if I'm just standing in her kitchen or sitting at her usual spot at the table, there's nowhere to hide from how much she's just... gone. That feels like it could completely overwhelm me, like I wouldn't be able to hold myself together at all.
therapist: There's something really tender and honest in what you just described — that the most frightening thing isn't other people's eyes on you, but your own unguarded encounter with her absence in the places that were most *hers*. I want to gently offer this: the fear that you "wouldn't be able to hold yourself together" assumes that falling apart in that moment would be something to survive rather than something that might actually be part of healing. What do you imagine would actually happen if you did let yourself feel the full weight of it — what's the worst your mind is predicting?

client: I think my mind is predicting that I'll just completely break down, like ugly crying in front of everyone, and then I won't be able to stop. And then everyone will be uncomfortable and trying to console me, and I'll end up feeling like I ruined the gathering and made it about me instead of just... being together as a family. I guess there's a lot of guilt wrapped up in that too, like grieving too visibly would somehow be a burden on everyone else.
therapist: There's so much compassion for others wrapped up in that fear — you're essentially trying to protect your family from your grief, even at the cost of carrying it entirely alone. But I want to gently turn something around: you noticed your aunt's tears at Thanksgiving, and did that ruin the gathering for you, or did it actually make you feel something real and human in that moment? I'm wondering if the "burden" you're afraid of becoming might actually be something your family would recognize as love for the same person they're all still missing too.

client: When you put it that way, my aunt's tears didn't ruin anything... if anything it made me feel less alone for a second, like we were both still holding onto her together. But I think there's still a part of me that feels like it's different when it's me, like I'm somehow more intense or more of a mess about it than everyone else. I don't fully know how to shake that feeling that my grief is too much, even if logically what you're saying makes sense.
therapist: You're holding something really important right now — your heart is starting to let in a new possibility, even while another part of you is still quietly insisting "yes, but not me, I'm the exception." That belief that your grief is *too much* is worth examining, because it's doing a lot of work to keep you feeling separate and undeserving of the same grace you so naturally extended to your aunt in that moment. Where do you think that feeling of being "too much" comes from — is this something that shows up for you beyond grief too, or does it feel specific to losing her?

client: Honestly, it's not specific to losing her... I think I've felt like "too much" in a lot of situations, like I always have this background sense that my emotions are bigger or harder to manage than other people's, and that I need to keep a lid on them to be acceptable. But I'm a little nervous about pulling on that thread, because it feels like a much bigger thing than just the family gatherings, and I came in here really just trying to get through those without falling apart.
therapist: It makes complete sense to feel a little cautious right now — you came in with a specific, painful problem, and suddenly there's a much larger door in front of you, and that can feel like more than you signed up for. I want to honor that, and also gently say: what you just named — this long-held sense that your emotions make you "too much" — might actually be the very thing that's been making the grief so much harder to bear, because you've been grieving *and* managing the belief that your grief is unacceptable at the same time. We don't have to go through that bigger door today, but I'm curious — does it feel like something worth coming back to, even if we focus on the gatherings for now?

client: Yeah, I think it probably is worth coming back to, even though part of me is already dreading it. But what you said about grieving and managing that belief at the same time... that actually landed in a way I wasn't expecting, because it does feel like twice the work, like I'm fighting on two fronts every time I feel sad. I'm still not fully convinced therapy is going to fix any of this, but I'm at least willing to keep showing up for now.
therapist: "Willing to keep showing up" is honestly enough — that's not a small thing, especially when part of you came in today not even sure this would be worth it. And I want to reflect back what you did here: you came in wanting to survive family gatherings, and you ended up uncovering something much deeper and more important about how you've been relating to your own emotions for a long time — that took real openness. As we keep going, I'd love to hold both threads together — the gatherings as something concrete to work toward, and that bigger pattern underneath — so it doesn't have to feel like two separate battles. How does that sound as a way to move forward?

client: That actually sounds more manageable than I expected, like I don't have to choose between dealing with the immediate thing and the bigger thing underneath it. I think I was afraid you'd want to just dive straight into my whole emotional history and leave me feeling more exposed than when I walked in. So yeah, holding both threads together... I can work with that, even if I'm still a little unsure about what that's actually going to look like in practice.
therapist: It's really good to hear that landed well — and your instinct to protect yourself from feeling unnecessarily exposed is actually a healthy one, not something to override. Good therapy shouldn't feel like being taken apart faster than you can put yourself back together, and I want you to know that you get to set the pace here. As a small, concrete step before we meet again, I'm wondering — would you be open to simply noticing the next time that "too much" feeling shows up for you, without trying to change it, just so we start to see it a little more clearly together?
